title: Grade 11 Chemistry — States of Matter
description: Chapter 5: gas laws, kinetic theory, real gases, Van der Waals equation
subject: chemistry

questions.question: Boyle's Law states that at constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is:
options: Directly proportional to its volume
Inversely proportional to its volume (P ∝ 1/V)
Independent of its volume
Equal to its volume divided by temperature
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: PV = constant at constant T and n. If volume halves, pressure doubles — useful for understanding gas compression and the behaviour of syringes.

questions.question: At STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure), the molar volume of an ideal gas is:
options: 11.2 L/mol
22.4 L/mol
44.8 L/mol
1 L/mol
questions.explanation: At STP (0°C, 1 atm), one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres. This is a fundamental constant in gas calculations.

questions.question: The ideal gas equation is:
options: PV = nRT
PV = RT
P = nRT/V²
PV² = nRT
questions.explanation: The ideal gas equation PV = nRT combines Boyle's, Charles's, and Avogadro's laws. P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = 8.314 J/mol·K, T = temperature in Kelvin.

questions.question: According to kinetic molecular theory, temperature is a measure of:
options: The total kinetic energy of all gas molecules
The average kinetic energy of gas molecules
The size of individual gas molecules
The number of molecules per unit volume
questions.explanation: Temperature (absolute, in Kelvin) is directly proportional to the average kinetic energy per molecule: KE_avg = (3/2)kT. Higher temperature means molecules move faster on average.

questions.question: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures states that:
options: The total volume of a gas mixture equals the sum of individual volumes
The total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of their partial pressures
Each gas in a mixture exerts zero pressure on the others
Gas molecules of different types cannot coexist in the same container
questions.explanation: P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ... Each gas in a mixture behaves independently and contributes its partial pressure proportional to its mole fraction.

questions.question: The Van der Waals equation modifies the ideal gas law to account for:
options: Only the finite volume of gas molecules
Both intermolecular attractive forces and the finite volume of gas molecules
Temperature variations at high pressure
The speed distribution of gas molecules
questions.explanation: Van der Waals equation: (P + an²/V²)(V - nb) = nRT. The 'a' term corrects for intermolecular attraction (reduces effective pressure); the 'b' term corrects for the volume occupied by molecules themselves.

questions.question: Graham's Law of Diffusion states that the rate of diffusion of a gas is:
options: Directly proportional to its molar mass
Inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass
Independent of molar mass
Directly proportional to its density
questions.explanation: r ∝ 1/√M. Lighter gases diffuse faster. This explains why hydrogen diffuses about 4× faster than oxygen (√32/√2 ≈ 4) and is used in uranium isotope separation.

questions.question: Which gas will effuse fastest according to Graham's Law?
options: CO₂ (M = 44 g/mol)
SO₂ (M = 64 g/mol)
CH₄ (M = 16 g/mol)
N₂ (M = 28 g/mol)
questions.explanation: CH₄ has the lowest molar mass (16 g/mol), so it diffuses/effuses fastest. Rate ∝ 1/√M: lighter = faster.

questions.question: What is the 'critical temperature' of a gas?
options: The temperature at which a gas instantly condenses
The temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied regardless of how much pressure is applied
The boiling point of the gas at 1 atm
The temperature at which gas molecules stop moving
questions.explanation: Above the critical temperature (Tc), kinetic energy overcomes intermolecular forces permanently and no amount of pressure can liquefy the gas. CO₂ has Tc = 304.2 K; H₂O has Tc = 647 K.

questions.question: The compressibility factor Z for a real gas at moderate pressure is less than 1 because:
options: Gas molecules have zero volume at moderate pressure
Intermolecular attractive forces reduce the effective pressure, making the gas more compressible than ideal
The gas expands more than expected due to high temperature
Z is always exactly 1 for any gas
questions.explanation: Z = PV/nRT. At moderate pressure, intermolecular attractions pull molecules together, reducing pressure below the ideal value — so Z < 1. At very high pressure, the repulsive volume effect dominates and Z > 1.

questions.question: Charles's Law states that at constant pressure, the volume of a gas:
options: Is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
Is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V ∝ T)
Decreases as temperature increases
Is independent of temperature
questions.explanation: Charles's Law: V/T = constant at constant P and n. Volume increases linearly with Kelvin temperature — this is why hot air balloons rise.

questions.question: The universal gas constant R has the value:
options: 8.314 J/mol·K only
0.0821 L·atm/mol·K only
1.987 cal/mol·K only
All of the above — they are different units of the same constant
questions.explanation: R = 8.314 J/mol·K = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K = 1.987 cal/mol·K. You choose the unit form that matches the other units in your problem.

questions.question: Brownian motion in colloidal suspensions provides evidence for:
options: Gravity acting on particles in solution
The continuous random motion of molecules (supporting kinetic molecular theory)
Electrical forces between particles
The solid-like nature of liquids at the molecular scale
questions.explanation: Brownian motion — the random zigzag movement of colloidal particles — is caused by unequal bombardment by surrounding solvent molecules. It was key evidence for the molecular theory of matter.

questions.question: The temperature of a gas is doubled from 300 K to 600 K at constant volume. What happens to its pressure?
options: Pressure halves
Pressure doubles
Pressure remains constant
Pressure increases by four times
questions.explanation: Gay-Lussac's Law: P/T = constant at constant V and n. If T doubles (300→600 K), P doubles. This is why pressure cookers must have safety valves.

questions.question: At absolute zero (0 K), the volume of an ideal gas would theoretically be:
options: Infinite — gases expand without limit
Maximum — the gas would be at its largest
Zero — all molecular motion ceases
Equal to 22.4 L regardless of amount
questions.explanation: By extrapolating Charles's Law, volume → 0 as T → 0 K. In reality, all gases liquefy before reaching 0 K, but the theoretical concept defines absolute zero and the Kelvin scale.

questions.question: Avogadro's Law states that at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases contain:
options: The same mass
The same number of molecules
Molecules of the same size
The same total kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Avogadro's Law: V ∝ n at constant T and P. One mole of any gas contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules (Avogadro's number) and occupies 22.4 L at STP.

questions.question: Which assumptions of kinetic molecular theory are violated by real gases?
options: That molecules have mass and move randomly — both are false for real gases
That molecules are point masses (no volume) and have no intermolecular forces — both are incorrect for real gases
That molecular speed increases with temperature — not true for real gases
That molecules move in straight lines — real gases have circular motion
questions.explanation: Real gas molecules do have finite volume and do exert forces on each other (van der Waals forces). These two deviations account for all differences between ideal and real gas behaviour.

questions.question: Liquefaction of gases is achieved by:
options: Heating the gas at constant pressure
Cooling below the critical temperature and applying sufficient pressure
Adding chemical reactants that absorb heat
Reducing the number of gas molecules in the container
questions.explanation: To liquefy a gas: first cool it below its critical temperature (Tc), then apply pressure. Above Tc, no amount of pressure can liquefy it. Liquid nitrogen (Tc = 126 K) and liquid oxygen (Tc = 155 K) are produced this way.

questions.question: A gas occupies 5 L at 1 atm. What volume will it occupy at 2 atm, at the same temperature?
options: 5 L
1 L
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. (1)(5) = (2)(V₂). V₂ = 5/2 = 2.5 L. Doubling pressure halves the volume.

questions.question: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows that for a gas at a given temperature:
options: All molecules have the same speed
Most molecules have speeds near the most probable speed, with very few at extremely high or low speeds
Half the molecules are stationary at any given moment
Molecular speed is independent of temperature
questions.explanation: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is a bell-shaped curve (skewed right) showing the distribution of molecular speeds. It gives three characteristic speeds: most probable (Vp), average (Vavg), and root mean square (Vrms).
